name: Anyway
tagline: You decide it's going to be a good night. Then you make it one.
epigraph: People tried everything to fix the orange in the Bronx cocktail. This is one more try.
language_row: Wren's Resonance on reading v4: ready. Sibling and cousin echoes cleared by 4-gram against every pour and every latest room draft: no entrance and no "nobody saw you" (the Angel); no getting ready, no empty room, no "happened by itself" (the Geisha); no "why it lasts" (the Nanny), "nobody left out" (the True Friend) or "It's usually you" (the Campaigner); "Then I added mine" checked against *Worth the Trip*'s "The rest is mine". Cut on the way: "the other way round" (the Reassurer), "how you look after people" (the Innovator), "come up with something" (the Nurse). One "I", no we/our/us, no bare "yours" for the drink, no guest pronouns; every "she"/"her" in yours 1–4 is Clara Bell Walsh (lint's four warnings, accepted by Wren). History is about 205 of yours' 424 words, just under half. ✓
sources: Studio fact card `_studio/fact-cards/clara-bell-walsh-cocktail-party.md` (*Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails*, COCKTAIL PARTY pdf 512, Eric Felten, read on the page; it cites the *Wichita Beacon*, 3 April 1917, p. 12, not read: Chronicling America blocked). The Bronx: Oxford BRONX pdf 358; David Wondrich, *Imbibe!* pdf 237–238 (Malloy's 1908 recipe in Boothby; the Akins line). Drink: *Flavor Matrix* pdf 80 (citrus aroma in the peel; coriander as a citrus note); Oxford GIN pdf 894 (coriander among London dry's usual botanicals); Oxford pdf 1750 (Peychaud's, the Sazerac's bitters); Oxford pdf 491; Dave Arnold, *Liquid Intelligence* (strength range); *Cocktail Codex* p. 64. Secondary, for the conflict on the meal only: Wayne Curtis, *The Long Bar*, 28 May 2025. Room notes: `work/jester-caregiver/`.
names_note: **Anyway**, the room's pick (all three, round 5): the word the person lives by ("Throw it anyway"), said in the reading before the glass says it; short across a bar ("An Anyway, please"). **The One That Took** (Wren's first) was set aside by Wren and Tomás because on a menu it reads as a claim that the drink fixed the Bronx, which Wren's own condition forbids and the record doesn't support (*Imbibe!* pdf 237). Also considered: *Another Go*, *Noon Till One* (Tomás), *Here's the Plan*, *Game for It* (Wren).
open_items: **The 1917 article itself wasn't read** (Chronicling America Cloudflare-blocked). Oxford pdf 512 is the only page under the story. "An instant hit" and "within weeks a St. Louis institution" are legend-grade (Wikipedia relaying Felten's paywalled 2007 *WSJ* column) and are kept out; the Country Club venue, the churchgoers and the newspaper's name are out too. If Robin can get the *Wichita Beacon* (3 April 1917, p. 12) or Felten's column, some could be promoted.
**The dinner is contested** (Oxford: dinner at one; Curtis 2025: light bites). The reading keeps only the hour, noon to one.

**Strength and acid at the edges:** 20.2% ABV (bottom of range) and 0.170% acid (above a spirit drink's ceiling, far below a sour's floor). Tomás's Checks justify both as the Bronx itself; Oxford's own 60/15/15 proportions read OUT on sugar and acid, so the sweet vermouth is raised to 30 ml. Gin must be 43% or stronger (40% reads OUT), and the wheel thin (about half a centimetre).

**Near miss, owned in Checks:** *Quite Alive* is also 60 gin to 30 sweet vermouth, but stirred with Fernet in a coupe. The Innocent family's Little Prince plan holds Martini · London dry · nick-and-nora, so this pour moved to a stemmed wine glass.

**Kept out on purpose:** the 1922 *Times* sneer (it mocks the drinking, not fun made on purpose), Wondrich's "I'll fix myself a Sazerac" (a 2007 author's taste), the "kiddie drinks" grumblers, the Waldorf and any Bronx inventor, and the sideboard coincidence (Oxford pdf 358; declined by Wren for history weight, kept here).
**y4 is the longest paragraph (156 words).** If Robin wants it shorter, Wren says the Bronx's two history clauses go first.
